title: Git sync holds the shared vault_write_lock across un-timed-out network fetch/push, so a slow or hanging remote blocks every HTTP and MCP vault write
affected: slow/hanging/unreachable git remote (dropped TLS, firewall blackhole, dead server)
any concurrent HTTP or MCP write while a sync is in flight
a remote that keeps the TCP connection open without responding
description: run_one_sync acquires the shared vault-mutation lock and holds it across spawn_blocking(...) calls. The runner performs git fetch/push via git2 without any timeout, so these calls block for as long as the remote keeps the socket alive. Every write handler blocks on vault_write_lock for that entire window. A persistently slow/hanging remote makes all note creation/edit/move/delete and attachment writes hang.
why: The adverse condition 'slow/failing/rejecting git remote' is explicitly in scope. Coupling the vault write-availability to the responsiveness of an external git remote is an availability failure.
fixSketch: Do the network phase (fetch/push) outside the vault_write_lock. Set a connect/transfer timeout on git2 fetch/push operations.

verdicts.reason: Lines 148-166 confirm run_one_sync acquires vault_lock.lock().await at line 149 and holds the guard until line 166, spanning the entire spawn_blocking call that invokes runner(...) (git fetch/push via git2) with no timeout wrapper anywhere in this function or run_loop. The mechanism as described is exactly what the code does.

Confirmed by reading src/git/task.rs:149-166: vault_lock is acquired at line 149 (_guard) and not dropped until line 166, which is after the .await on spawn_blocking (line 159) that runs the git2 fetch/push (via runner(...)) and unpushed_count. No timeout wraps this call. A hanging/slow remote therefore blocks the lock release indefinitely, and any other task calling vault_lock.lock().await (HTTP write handlers, MCP write tools) is blocked for the same unbounded duration. This is a genuine availability failure under the stated adverse condition, not mitigated by any timeout, cancellation, or lock-scoping in the visible code.

Confirmed by reading src/git/task.rs:128-166: run_one_sync acquires vault_lock at line 149 (_guard) before calling tokio::task::spawn_blocking which runs runner(...) doing the actual git2 fetch/push network I/O, and the lock is not dropped until line 166 after the blocking task completes. There is no timeout wrapping the spawn_blocking call, no tokio::time::timeout, and no evidence of any retry/circuit-breaker that would bound this. The comment on line 148 ('Hold the vault lock across the blocking git work so no MCP write races it') shows this coupling is deliberate but does not mitigate the availability risk described. No other guard in this file limits git2 network call duration, so a hanging remote genuinely blocks vault_lock acquisition for all HTTP/MCP writers indefinitely. Severity as high is reasonable given full write-path stall. Not refuted.

title: A crash between a vault file write and its debounced git commit strands the edit out of git, and the stranded dirty file later makes every merge-requiring sync fail
affected: process crash/kill between atomic_write and the next debounced git sync
then the remote moving ahead so a later sync needs a merge
description: Write handlers write the vault file to disk and enqueue a WriteRecord onto an in-memory channel that is only drained after debounce. If the process is killed in that window, the file is on disk but the WriteRecord is lost. On restart, startup_flush only runs when has_unpushed is true, which compares local vs remote commits. A stranded file is a modified tracked file, so the next sync that must integrate remote changes hits dirty_tracked_files and aborts.
why: 'Process crash mid-operation' is a named adverse condition. The coordination between volatile write-record queue and durable vault leaves changes silently un-synced.
fixSketch: On startup reconcile actual working-tree status against git: if git status shows dirty tracked files, stage+commit them. Alternatively persist pending WriteRecords.

verdicts.reason: GitSyncHandle::record (line 23) matches the claim: it only pushes onto an unbounded in-memory mpsc channel and its own doc comment says it 'drops silently if the background task has stopped.' Nothing durable is written here, and the crash-recovery path (startup_flush at lines 48-51/87-89) is gated purely on has_unpushed comparing local vs remote commits, not on whether a WriteRecord was queued. The described gap between file write and channel enqueue durability is real as far as this file's mechanics go.

title: A panic while the SqliteCache writer Mutex is held poisons it permanently, killing all future reindexes and cache writes for the process lifetime
affected: any panic inside the reindex transaction while holding the writer lock
e.g. bytemuck::cast_slice on a corrupted/partially-written chunk_vectors blob
description: SqliteCache.conn is a std::sync::Mutex. replace_from_index_with_embedder holds the guard for the entire reindex transaction. preserve_existing_vectors does bytemuck::cast_slice, which panics if blob length is not a multiple of 4. Any panic there poisons the Mutex permanently.
why: A single panic converts a transient fault into a permanent process-wide degradation with no self-recovery.
fixSketch: Recover from poisoned lock instead of propagating error indefinitely. Guard preserve_existing_vectors against non-multiple-of-4 blob lengths.

verdicts.reason: conn is a std::sync::Mutex<Connection> (line 12, line 32), and connection() (line 164) simply maps a poison error to a string via lock().map_err(...) rather than recovering/clearing the poison (e.g. via into_inner or a parking_lot mutex). Since std::sync::Mutex poisoning is permanent for the mutex's lifetime, any panic while the guard is held (e.g. during the cited reindex-transaction scenario) would indeed make every subsequent connection() call fail for the rest of the process. The mechanism claimed is real in this code.
